title: How to Use AI to Give Every Student a Voice in Class Discussion
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: Phillip Alcock gives teachers a step-by-step method for running silent debates, using Google NotebookLM to generate an alternating PRO and CON slide deck from a single two-sided article. He argues that ordinary class debates reward confident talkers, whereas a written, five-round format makes every student engage with every argument. The guide covers choosing a source with real evidence on both sides, giving each topic its own notebook, entering a structured prompt in the customisation field, checking every slide before class, and delivery options including a visible timer or a shared link. It is a practical classroom AI workflow with reflective pause points, though it is interleaved with promotion of paid membership.
points: Silent debate gives the quietest students a voice by making writing the only voice in the room across five timed rounds.
NotebookLM works from a single bounded source, so each debate topic needs its own notebook to avoid pulling arguments from the wrong material.
The prompt entered in the customisation field controls the whole deck structure, including alternating PRO and CON slides, evidence limits and round footers.
The teacher should review every slide against a checklist and regenerate with a sharper question if the CON side feels thin.
quotes: There’s a student in most classrooms who could run rings around the loud ones intellectually, but they’ll never say so out loud. They are working out their argument right as someone else states it badly, and then the discussion moves on. Traditional class debates are, in practice, a performance sport for the confident.
In a silent debate, every student engages with every argument, in writing, on their own sheet, for every five-minute round. No raised hands. No dominant voices. Writing is the only voice in the room.
A debatable article with genuine two-sided potential. It needs real facts, quotes, or data that can support arguments on both sides of a question, not an opinion piece pushing one direction.

Each debate topic gets its own notebook. This matters. Mixing topics in a single notebook causes NotebookLM to pull arguments from the wrong source material (slide 6 identifies this as the most common structural error).

The source article is the only content NotebookLM draws from. As slide 4 explains, NotebookLM doesn’t access the internet or its training data during generation. Every argument on every slide traces directly to what you uploaded. Language calibrates to the source. You can present the output without additional fact-checking.
The Sources panel shows the article title, a green checkmark, and a brief AI-generated summary. Read that summary. Confirm it actually reflects your article’s topic, not something generic.
Click Generate. The Studio panel displays “Generating slide deck… based on 1 source.” Generation takes 3–10 minutes depending on article length and server load.
